> A device that detects exoplanet transits by measuring the brightness of a star. When a planet passes in front of its star, the star's brightness drops slightly. The photodiode captures the light, the op-amp amplifies the signal, and the Arduino records the light curve.

Designed the schematic and researched components for the Exoplanet Transit Detector. I chose the BPW34 photodiode because it has low dark current (2 nA) and a wide spectral range (400-1100 nm). I selected the LM358 op-amp to amplify the weak signal from the photodiode. I also planned the connection between the Arduino, the OLED display, and the power source. This session helped me understand how the detector will work as a system.

### 2026-10-02 — ![Screenshot_20261002_115147_ru.yandex.searchplugin](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/2hMkAHC5MI9iXNob1mUuGpOiwCBjOBzd/57b7d7ef9e8e0ec5c3e5f72d888e0a58fac6779d9b4365b50

**3h**

![Screenshot_20261002_115147_ru.yandex.searchplugin](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/2hMkAHC5MI9iXNob1mUuGpOiwCBjOBzd/57b7d7ef9e8e0ec5c3e5f72d888e0a58fac6779d9b4365b504f82d02f4d9fbc3.jpg)

Today I focused on component selection and sourcing for the Exoplanet Transit Detector. I spent time researching each part to make sure it fits the project requirements and stays within the $65 budget.

First, I chose the BPW34 photodiode because of its low dark current (2 nA) and wide spectral range (400-1100 nm). This is important because the detector needs to measure small changes in starlight without picking up too much noise.

Second, I selected the LM358 op-amp to amplify the weak signal from the photodiode. I calculated the gain using R1 = 1 kΩ and R2 = 100 kΩ, which gives a gain of 100. This means the tiny current from the photodiode becomes a voltage the Arduino can read.

Third, I found an Arduino Nano V3 with the ATmega328P chip. It has 32 KB of memory and a 10-bit ADC, which gives a resolution of about 4.9 mV per step (5V / 1024). This is enough to detect small changes in brightness.

Fourth, I chose a 0.96" OLED display with I2C interface (128x64 pixels). It will show the light curve in real time.

Finally, I added a resistor kit, capacitor kit, jumper wires, and a plastic project box. The total cost is about $42, which fits within the $65 budget.

I learned how to read datasheets, compare specifications, and choose components that work together as a system.
